section_1.title: Prerequisite: The Cartesian Stage
section_1.content: Establish the 2D coordinate system (x, y axes) as the environment. Explain the difference between a 'point' (a fixed location) and a 'vector' (an instruction for movement).
section_1.example: Visualize a grid-based map. A 'point' is where a Treasure Chest is buried at (3, 2). A 'vector' is the instruction to a Robot: 'Move 3 units right and 2 units up'.

section_2.title: Defining the Vector: Magnitude and Direction
section_2.content: Define a vector as an object with two essential properties: Magnitude (length/size) and Direction (where it points). Introduce the arrow notation.
section_2.example: An Airplane (the device) flying at 500 km/h toward the North-East. The speed is the magnitude, and North-East is the direction. If either changes, the vector changes.

section_3.title: Component Form: The DNA of a Vector
section_3.content: Show how to break a vector into its horizontal (x) and vertical (y) parts. Introduce the bracket notation [x, y]. This bridges geometry with algebra.
section_3.example: A Frog leaps from (0,0) to (4,3). We write this vector as v = [4, 3]. Visually, we draw a right-angled triangle with a base of 4 and a height of 3 to show how the jump is composed.

section_4.title: Vector Addition: The Tip-to-Tail Method
section_4.content: Explain how to combine two vectors. Graphically, place the 'tail' of the second vector at the 'tip' of the first. Algebraically, add the corresponding components.
section_4.example: A Cat walks 3 units East (Vector A), then 2 units North (Vector B). The resulting displacement (Vector A + B) is a diagonal line from the start to the final position: [3+0, 0+2] = [3, 2].

section_5.title: Scalar Multiplication: Scaling the Force
section_5.content: Introduce 'Scalars' (regular numbers). Explain how multiplying a vector by a scalar changes its magnitude but keeps (or reverses) its direction. This is 'scaling'.
section_5.example: A Superhero is flying with a velocity vector v = [1, 1]. Suddenly, they use a 'Speed Boost' x 3. The new vector is 3v = [3, 3]. The arrow gets three times longer in the same direction.

section_6.title: Real-World Application: Force Fields
section_6.content: Conclude by showing how vectors represent forces in the real world, leading into more complex linear algebra topics like Dot Products or Vector Spaces.
section_6.example: A boat trying to cross a river. The boat's engine vector points straight across, but the river's current vector points downstream. The actual path of the boat is the 'Sum Vector' of both forces.

section_1.title: Prerequisite: The Cartesian Stage
section_1.content: Establish the 2D coordinate system (x, y axes) as the environment. Explain the difference between a 'point' (a fixed location) and a 'vector' (an instruction for movement).
section_1.example: Visualize a grid-based map. A 'point' is where a Treasure Chest is buried at (3, 2). A 'vector' is the instruction to a Robot: 'Move 3 units right and 2 units up'.

section_2.title: Defining the Vector: Magnitude and Direction
section_2.content: Define a vector as an object with two essential properties: Magnitude (length/size) and Direction (where it points). Introduce the arrow notation.
section_2.example: An Airplane (the device) flying at 500 km/h toward the North-East. The speed is the magnitude, and North-East is the direction. If either changes, the vector changes.

section_3.title: Component Form: The DNA of a Vector
section_3.content: Show how to break a vector into its horizontal (x) and vertical (y) parts. Introduce the bracket notation [x, y]. This bridges geometry with algebra.
section_3.example: A Frog leaps from (0,0) to (4,3). We write this vector as v = [4, 3]. Visually, we draw a right-angled triangle with a base of 4 and a height of 3 to show how the jump is composed.

section_4.title: Vector Addition: The Tip-to-Tail Method
section_4.content: Explain how to combine two vectors. Graphically, place the 'tail' of the second vector at the 'tip' of the first. Algebraically, add the corresponding components.
section_4.example: A Cat walks 3 units East (Vector A), then 2 units North (Vector B). The resulting displacement (Vector A + B) is a diagonal line from the start to the final position: [3+0, 0+2] = [3, 2].

section_5.title: Scalar Multiplication: Scaling the Force
section_5.content: Introduce 'Scalars' (regular numbers). Explain how multiplying a vector by a scalar changes its magnitude but keeps (or reverses) its direction. This is 'scaling'.
section_5.example: A Superhero is flying with a velocity vector v = [1, 1]. Suddenly, they use a 'Speed Boost' x 3. The new vector is 3v = [3, 3]. The arrow gets three times longer in the same direction.

section_6.title: Real-World Application: Force Fields
section_6.content: Conclude by showing how vectors represent forces in the real world, leading into more complex linear algebra topics like Dot Products or Vector Spaces.
section_6.example: A boat trying to cross a river. The boat's engine vector points straight across, but the river's current vector points downstream. The actual path of the boat is the 'Sum Vector' of both forces.

section_2.title: Defining the Vector: Magnitude and Direction
lecture_lines: Meet the vector: a mathematical arrow with two traits.

section_3.title: Component Form: The DNA of a Vector
lecture_lines: Every vector breaks down into horizontal and vertical parts.
First, we identify the horizontal move along the x-axis.
Next, we measure the vertical move along the y-axis.
We write these components inside square brackets like this.
These parts form a right triangle with the vector.
animations: Draw a cyan #00FFFF vector from (0,0) to (4,3) and label it 'v'. self.wait(2).
Highlight the x-component with an orange #FF8800 line and label 'x=4'. self.wait(1.5).
Highlight the y-component with a green #00FF00 line and label 'y=3'. self.wait(1.5).

section_4.title: Vector Addition: The Tip-to-Tail Method
lecture_lines: To combine vectors, we use the tip-to-tail method.
Place the second vector's tail at the first's tip.
The resulting vector connects the very start to the end.
Algebraically, we simply add the corresponding x and y parts.
This sum represents the total displacement of both movements.
animations: Draw Vector A in cyan #00FFFF and Vector B in magenta #FF00FF from the origin. self.wait(2).
Shift the magenta #FF00FF Vector B so its tail meets Vector A's tip. self.wait(2).
Draw a white #FFFFFF dashed line from the origin to the new tip of B. self.wait(1.5).
Reveal the solid white #FFFFFF resultant vector and label it 'A + B'. self.wait(2).
Highlight the 'A + B' label with a SurroundingRectangle in white #FFFFFF. self.wait(2).

section_5.title: Scalar Multiplication: Scaling the Force
lecture_lines: Scalars are regular numbers that scale our vectors.

This scaling allows us to stretch or shrink any arrow.
animations: Draw a cyan #00FFFF vector v = [1,1] on the grid. self.wait(2).

section_6.title: Real-World Application: Force Fields
lecture_lines: In reality, vectors represent forces like wind or gravity.

from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        title = "Vector Addition: The Tip-to-Tail Method"
        lines = [
            "To combine vectors, we use the tip-to-tail method.",
            "Place the second vector's tail at the first's tip.",
            "The resulting vector connects the very start to the end.",
            "Algebraically, we simply add the corresponding x and y parts.",
            "This sum represents the total displacement of both movements."
        ]
        self.setup_layout(title, lines)

        # Define key grid positions for the animation
        # We start with origin at D2, A extends to D5 (length 3), B extends to B2 (length 2)
        origin_pos = self.grid["D2"]
        a_tip_pos = self.grid["D5"]
        b_tip_pos = self.grid["B2"]
        b_shifted_tip_pos = self.grid["B5"]

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Draw Vector A in cyan #00FFFF and Vector B in magenta #FF00FF from the origin.
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#00FFFF")
        
        vec_a = Arrow(start=origin_pos, end=a_tip_pos, buff=0, color="#00FFFF", stroke_width=4)
        vec_b = Arrow(start=origin_pos, end=b_tip_pos, buff=0, color="#FF00FF", stroke_width=4)
        
        label_a = MathTex("A", color="#00FFFF")
        self.place_at_grid(label_a, "E3", scale_factor=0.8) # Positioned below Vector A
        
        label_b = MathTex("B", color="#FF00FF")
        self.place_at_grid(label_b, "C1", scale_factor=0.8) # Positioned left of Vector B

        self.play(Create(vec_a), Write(label_a))
        self.play(Create(vec_b), Write(label_b))
        self.wait(2)

        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#FF00FF")

            FadeOut(dashed_res),
            Create(vec_res),
            Write(label_res)

        self.wait(2)

        self.lecture[4].set_color("#FFFFFF")

section_1.title: Prerequisite: The Cartesian Stage
section_1.content: Establish the 2D coordinate system (x, y axes) as the environment. Explain the difference between a 'point' (a fixed location) and a 'vector' (an instruction for movement).
section_1.example: Visualize a grid-based map. A 'point' is where a Treasure Chest is buried at (3, 2). A 'vector' is the instruction to a Robot: 'Move 3 units right and 2 units up'.

section_2.title: Defining the Vector: Magnitude and Direction
section_2.content: Define a vector as an object with two essential properties: Magnitude (length/size) and Direction (where it points). Introduce the arrow notation.
section_2.example: An Airplane (the device) flying at 500 km/h toward the North-East. The speed is the magnitude, and North-East is the direction. If either changes, the vector changes.

section_3.title: Component Form: The DNA of a Vector
section_3.content: Show how to break a vector into its horizontal (x) and vertical (y) parts. Introduce the bracket notation [x, y]. This bridges geometry with algebra.
section_3.example: A Frog leaps from (0,0) to (4,3). We write this vector as v = [4, 3]. Visually, we draw a right-angled triangle with a base of 4 and a height of 3 to show how the jump is composed.

section_4.title: Vector Addition: The Tip-to-Tail Method
section_4.content: Explain how to combine two vectors. Graphically, place the 'tail' of the second vector at the 'tip' of the first. Algebraically, add the corresponding components.
section_4.example: A Cat walks 3 units East (Vector A), then 2 units North (Vector B). The resulting displacement (Vector A + B) is a diagonal line from the start to the final position: [3+0, 0+2] = [3, 2].

section_5.title: Scalar Multiplication: Scaling the Force
section_5.content: Introduce 'Scalars' (regular numbers). Explain how multiplying a vector by a scalar changes its magnitude but keeps (or reverses) its direction. This is 'scaling'.
section_5.example: A Superhero is flying with a velocity vector v = [1, 1]. Suddenly, they use a 'Speed Boost' x 3. The new vector is 3v = [3, 3]. The arrow gets three times longer in the same direction.

section_6.title: Real-World Application: Force Fields
section_6.content: Conclude by showing how vectors represent forces in the real world, leading into more complex linear algebra topics like Dot Products or Vector Spaces.
section_6.example: A boat trying to cross a river. The boat's engine vector points straight across, but the river's current vector points downstream. The actual path of the boat is the 'Sum Vector' of both forces.
